articles.title: Przewalski's horses disappeared from Kazakhstan for 200 years; two foals have now been born as conservationists rebuild the wild population
articles.summary: In the early hours of 22 August, a seven-year-old Przewalski's horse gave birth at the Alibi Reintroduction Centre, a wildlife sanctuary on Kazakhstan's
articles.body: In the early hours of 22 August, a seven-year-old Przewalski's horse gave birth at the Alibi Reintroduction Centre, a wildlife sanctuary on Kazakhstan's steppe. According to the United Nations Environment Programme, experts believe the male foal may be the first Przewalski's horse born on these grasslands in two centuries. Eight days after that birth, Umbra, a six-year-old mare, gave birth to another male. The last of the horses was spotted in the wild in 1969, roaming the Gobi Desert. Since 2024, 22 horses have been airlifted from European zoos to the centre, and officials want 40 horses by 2029.How many Przewalski’s horses were bornConservationist Albert Salemgareyev received an excited call from a colleague in the early morning hours of 22 August. A seven-year-old Przewalski's horse, one of the rarest equines in the world, had just given birth at the sanctuary. Salemgareyev, who leads the effort to return Przewalski's horses to the wild, then drove 12 hours from Kazakhstan's capital, Astana, to the Alibi Reintroduction Centre.When he arrived, the foal, still a little shaky on its feet, was huddled beside its mother. "For me, it was a very emotional moment," Salemgareyev says. "It's not just another horse for me. It's the beginning of a new generation here in Kazakhstan." UNEP adds that eight days after the mare Tessa gave birth to her history-making foal, Umbra, a six-year-old mare gave birth to another male. Neither foal has been named yet.Why did Przewalski’s horses nearly go extinctPrzewalski's horses once roamed the plains of Central Asia in large numbers, their short, stocky bodies ideal for retaining heat during the region's brutal winters. By the mid-1900s, hunting, habitat loss from farming and competition from livestock had decimated the herds. UNEP records that the last of the horses was spotted in the wild in 1969, roaming the Gobi Desert alone.The animals survived in European zoos, where an elaborate breeding programme helped keep their genetic pool diverse and intact. Conservationists say this is important because the horses occupy a unique branch of the equine family tree. They have two more chromosomes than other horses and, unlike free-roaming horses in Australia and the United States of America, have never been domesticated. So-called "wild" horses such as mustangs are the feral offspring of domesticated horses. Experts consider Przewalski's horses the world's last truly wild horses, and the animals are hard to handle and almost impossible to ride.How is Kazakhstan restoring its steppeThe Kazakh government launched an effort in 2005 to restore 75,000 square kilometres of steppe and semi-desert that had been damaged by overgrazing, unsustainable farming practices and climate change. Known as the Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative, the longstanding partnership has been named a UN World Restoration Flagship, an award that honours ground-breaking efforts to revive natural spaces. Conservationists focused first on bolstering populations of endangered saiga antelope and the kulan, a type of wild ass. UNEP reports that hundreds of thousands of saiga now roam the Kazakh steppe.Salemgareyev and colleagues then turned to the Przewalski's horse. Since 2024, 22 horses have been airlifted from European zoos to the reintroduction centre. There, in a series of fenced enclosures, the animals are taught how to live in the wild, with conservationists showing them how to dig in the snow to find food, among other things. Susan Gardner, Director of the Ecosystems Division at UNEP, says: "The community-based protection of these rangelands that led to the birth of this foal is one of the great conservation success stories of the last decade." She adds: "It shows that when we put our minds to it, we can restore ecosystems and give species a second chance."How quickly do Przewalski’s foals growThe foals were standing and drinking from their mothers within 30 minutes of being born. A few days later they were trying to jump and gallop, and by their third week, according to Salemgareyev, they had nearly doubled in size. Przewalski's horses live in small groups of five to 10 animals known as a harem. Over the coming weeks, conservationists will monitor how the other harem members react to the foals and track whether Tessa and Umbra show their offspring how to drink water, taste herbs for edibility and sound the alarm for predators.Both foals, who have the same father, a stallion named Zorro, will remain with their harems in a 56-hectare enclosure for now. Zorro died in 2025, and the big test will come next year, when a new stallion is introduced to the harems. In the wild, stallions have been known to harass or even kill the offspring of other males. If the transition goes well, UNEP reports, the horses should be released into the wild at the beginning of May. Conservation officials want to have 40 horses in Kazakhstan by 2029, with the end goal of establishing a stable, free-roaming population that does not need human intervention. "When you see a horse on the steppe, it looks like it belongs on the steppe," Salemgareyev says.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Google CEO Sundar Pichai announces EmbeddingGemma 2 model; says it is company’s first open, natively multimodal embedding model
articles.summary: Google has launched EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model for devices.
articles.body: Google has launched EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model for devices. The launch comes a year after the company introduced EmbeddingGemma for developers last year. For those unaware, an embedding model is a machine learning tool that turns complex data like words, sentences, images, or audio into a list of numbers called a vector. Built on the Gemma 4 architecture and released under a commercially permissive Apache 2.0 license, EmbeddingGemma 2 has 740 million parameters, making it optimal for on-device inference. It can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query, all processed by a single, natively multimodal model.Announcing the new model, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said: “Introducing EmbeddingGemma 2, a new open multimodal model that sets the standard for on-device efficiency.- our first open, natively multimodal embedding model- handles text, code, image, video, and audio tasks within a lightweight, modular 740M parameter form factor- ideal for offline, privacy-first RAG when paired with Gemma 4- outperforms some specialist models more than twice its sizeWeights available now on Hugging Face.”EmbeddingGemma 2: Key capabilitiesEmbeddingGemma 2 is designed to provide a single, compact open model released under the Apache 2.0 license, delivering exceptional multimodal performance for its size. Based on Gemma 4, this sub-1B model maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a unified 768-dimensional space. Its modular architecture can scale from 270M parameters for text and code up to 740M parameters for all modalities. Key capabilities of the EmbeddingGemma include:Native multimodal retrieval: Unlocks search across text, code, images, video, and audio directly in a shared 768-dimensional vector space.Superior code understanding: Significantly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1 on code search and technical retrieval, making it ideal for local codebase indexing and agentic code search.Modular memory footprint: Selectively load only the encoders you need at runtime: 270M (text/code), 440M (text + vision), 570M (text + audio), or 740M (full multimodal), all projecting into the same compatible vector space.Flexible vector storage: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) enables dynamic truncation from 768 dimensions down to 128 dimensions, cutting vector database storage requirements while retaining much of the original quality. For instance, at 256 dimensions, most of the full quality of the original embedding on text and code is retained and about 95% on image, video, and speech retrievalHow it worksGoogle says that all inputs are processed through the shared backbone and their resulting embeddings occupy the same dimensional space:Text and code (270M base): An adapted Gemma 4 decoder with an 8,192-token context window.Vision (+170M): A vision encoder that processes images, visual documents (PDFs, slides, charts), and video frames.Audio (+300M): A dedicated speech and sound encoder that directly ingests raw audio.Modular loading: You only load what you need. Run text-only at 270M parameters, add vision for 440M parameters, or load the full multimodal model at 740M parameters.Shared tokenizer & audio encoder with Gemma 4: When paired with Gemma 4 in an on-device RAG pipeline, both models share the same text tokenizer and audio encoder architecture, reducing the total memory footprint.You use AI every day. articles.title: And thereby hangs a tale! Jeffrey Archer’s Delhi connect
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Delhi traffic signal was the starting point of a love story in Jeffrey Archer’s ‘Caste-Off’.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Delhi traffic signal was the starting point of a love story in Jeffrey Archer’s ‘Caste-Off’. Jamwal and Nisha fall for each other while waiting for the light to turn green.Archer, the English novelist and politician who died Monday at 86, had connections with the Indian capital beyond the pages of his books. He met readers at a Delhi airport book-signing session in 2015 and addressed an audience ranging from children to senior citizens at Siri Fort Auditorium in 2019.The city also made an impression on him beyond its fictional possibilities.Asked what he liked about Delhi in a June 2010 interview with TOI, Archer praised the layout of its centre and its parliamentary precinct. “I was very impressed with that,” he said.His admiration was coupled with amusement at Delhi’s traffic scene. In the same interview, he expressed astonishment at the nature of Indian driving and joked about motorists’ treatment of lane markings.At the interactive session at Siri Fort, he discussed ‘Kane and Abel’, his debut novel ‘Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less’, and the origins of ‘The Clifton Chronicles’, before signing books for his Delhi fans.For some in that audience, the memories have proved as enduring as Archer’s books. Sonalika Paul, an avid reader and private-sector employee who has since moved to Canada, still remembers an anecdote he shared that evening.He recalled a boy approaching his car in Mumbai with a stack of books and asking whether he wanted the latest Jeffrey Archer. The author’s response: “I am the latest Jeffrey Archer.”Paul says, “That story stayed with me. In that one exchange, you could see both his humour and how far his books had travelled.”The evening at Siri Fort also offered readers a glimpse of the man behind his plot twists. Archer opened with cricket, speaking about Indian players and praising Virat Kohli, before describing a writing routine that still involved putting every word down by hand. For aspiring authors, there was also a reminder of the persistence behind his success: he recalled 16 publishers rejecting his first novel and spoke of the years of work, determination and luck that a writing career demanded.For Dr Jonathan Koshy Varghese, assistant professor of English at DU’s Lady Shri Ram College, Archer was among the authors who introduced him to a wider world of books as a teenager. His novels were discoveries made in school libraries, bridging changing reading tastes. “I read him when I was bored with Enid Blyton and when I needed something lighter than Mario Puzo,” he says.For Varghese, Archer’s death closes a chapter in a generation’s reading life, even as its readers continue to turn to other books. “Archer represented a kind of reading that was guilt-free,” the professor says — an inexpensive indulgence, enjoyed for the sheer pleasure of reading a good story.That connection with readers helped turn Archer’s releases into eagerly awaited events. Aninda Das, who has worked with leading publishing houses, recalls the anticipation whenever a new Archer title reached bookstores. “An Archer book hitting bookshelves was an occasion in itself, and that excitement has endured for decades,” he said, describing the lasting affection and loyalty that the author commanded among Indian readers.For avid reader Piyush Amola, Archer’s appeal began with the urge to turn another page. “With Archer, you always wanted to know what happened next. His language was easy, but his plots kept you guessing,” he says. The ambition, rivalries and family loyalties made the stories feel familiar, Amola adds, even when they unfolded in worlds far removed from his own. “You finished one book and looked forward to the next.”You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Texas man faces execution for killing convenience store clerk in 2000
articles.summary: A Texas man convicted of killing a convenience store clerk in 2000 is set to be executed by lethal injection on Wednesday.
articles.body: A Texas man convicted of killing a convenience store clerk in 2000 is set to be executed by lethal injection on Wednesday. If carried out, it would be the 30th execution in the US this year.Jamaal Howard, 46, was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Vickie Swartout, 42. She was shot once in the chest during a robbery at a store in Silsbee, a small town about 161 km northeast of Houston.Howard was 20 when the killing took place. According to court records cited by news agency Associated Press, he took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store. Surveillance video presented during the trial showed Howard shooting Swartout.Howard's lawyers have argued that he is intellectually disabled and should not be executed. The state has argued that he has not provided enough evidence to support the claim.Howard has also asked the US Supreme Court to stop the execution.The Supreme Court barred the execution of people with intellectual disabilities in 2002, but allowed states some discretion in deciding whether a person meets the criteria.If Howard's execution goes ahead, he will be the seventh person executed in Texas this year. Two more executions are currently scheduled in the state.The execution would come after a failed attempt last week to execute Christa Pike in Tennessee. Pike's lawyers said on Tuesday that she remained awake and was speaking while receiving treatment at a hospital.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Priscilla Chan’s fund gave $330,000 to Kauaʻi schools; all 23 public and charter schools received flexible grants for the new academic year
articles.summary: Priscilla Chan’s fund has provided $330,000 to support Kauaʻi’s schools as the new academic year gets underway, with all 23 public and charter schools
articles.body: Priscilla Chan’s fund has provided $330,000 to support Kauaʻi’s schools as the new academic year gets underway, with all 23 public and charter schools receiving a share of the funding. The unrestricted grants give school leaders flexibility to direct the money towards their most pressing needs. As reported by Hawaii News Now, the support also extends to Kumu’s Cupboard, a Līhuʻe nonprofit that provides free classroom supplies to teachers. The latest funding continues the Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi Community Fund’s support for the island, established in 2019. Separately, Chan and Mark Zuckerberg have also backed a free back-to-school event that distributed more than 3,000 supply-filled backpacks to local students.Priscilla Chan’s $330,000 Kauaʻi schools funding gives all 23 schools flexibilityThe latest grants cover Kauaʻi’s full public and charter school network, including 16 public schools and seven public charter schools. Rather than being tied to a particular classroom project or a narrowly defined expense, the funding is unrestricted.That gives individual school leaders room to decide how the money should be used. Needs can differ from one school to another, and flexible funding allows those decisions to be made locally rather than according to a single island-wide spending plan.Kauaʻi Complex Area Superintendent Leila Maeda-Kobayashi said, “Unrestricted or flexible grants empower our school leaders to direct resources exactly where they are needed most.”For schools preparing for a new academic year, that flexibility can matter. Expenses are not always the same from one campus to the next, and unrestricted support can be directed towards practical requirements as they arise.Priscilla Chan’s fund helps Kumu’s Cupboard provide free school suppliesThe funding is not limited to schools themselves. Kumu’s Cupboard, based in Līhuʻe, is also among the recipients. The nonprofit provides classroom supplies free of charge to teachers and other educational staff throughout the year. Its role is separate from the individual schools, but its work is closely connected to the day-to-day costs educators can face when putting together lessons and classroom activities.Including the organisation in the grant distribution broadens the reach of the funding beyond school campuses. It also means teachers can access supplies through a community organisation rather than relying solely on resources allocated to their schools.Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi fund continues its community support for schoolsThe Chan Zuckerberg Kauai Community Fund was established in 2019 as a way of supporting community needs on the island. The fund operates through the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation, which administers the latest grants.The new distribution comes at the beginning of the 2026-27 school year, when schools, families and educators are again dealing with the costs associated with returning to class. Hawaiʻi Community Foundation Program Director Marissa Sandblom said, “By addressing resource disparities and financial pressures facing students, families, and educators, we can help remove barriers and cultivate the necessary conditions for meaningful engagement in learning.”The decision to provide unrestricted grants is significant in practical terms because schools can determine where the money is most useful rather than receiving funding that can only be spent on a predetermined programme.Priscilla Chan’s fund extends Kauaʻi school support through free suppliesThe fund's support has also extended into a community back-to-school event. Reportedly, Priscilla Chan and Mark Zuckerberg joined other local donors in sponsoring Kukui Grove’s Back to School Bash. The event is described by organisers as Kauaʻi’s largest free school supply giveaway. More than 3,000 backpacks, each filled with school supplies, were distributed to K-12 students. That initiative provides a more direct form of assistance for families. While the school grants are managed at an institutional level, the giveaway puts supplies directly into the hands of students preparing to return to classrooms.Taken together, the two forms of support cover different parts of the school community. The grants give schools and an education-focused nonprofit greater control over resources, while the giveaway helps students with some of the basic supplies needed for the new school year.$330,000 from Priscilla Chan’s fund reaches all 23 Kauaʻi schoolsThe scale of the latest funding is partly defined by its coverage. All 23 public and charter schools on Kauaʻi are included, rather than a selected group of campuses. It also reflects the fund’s wider community focus, which has continued since its establishment in 2019.For the schools receiving the unrestricted grants, the next step is deciding how that money can best be used locally. For Kumu’s Cupboard, the funding adds support for its ongoing supply programme. And for the thousands of students who received backpacks at the Back to School Bash, the benefit was more immediate: school materials to take with them as classes began.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kharge to host INDIA bloc lunch as opposition plans next move after ‘vote chori’ protest
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A day after INDIA bloc MPs marched towards the Election Commission and Rahul Gandhi staged an hours-long sit-in, Congress president Mallikarjun
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A day after INDIA bloc MPs marched towards the Election Commission and Rahul Gandhi staged an hours-long sit-in, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge is set to host opposition MPs for lunch in Delhi.Kharge has invited INDIA bloc MPs for lunch at 1.30 pm at Sagar Ratna on Janpath, sources informed ANI. The MPs are also expected to sign a letter seeking a meeting with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.The meeting comes after a dramatic day of protests on Tuesday, when opposition MPs marched from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters, demanding a meeting with the election commissioners over their allegations of irregularities in the electoral process.What happened on TuesdayThe march was stopped by Delhi Police near Akashvani Bhawan, after which opposition MPs staged a sit-in. Rahul Gandhi, along with Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other Congress leaders, had entered the Akashvani Bhawan premises and insisted that the delegation be allowed to meet the election commissioners.The protest continued for nearly nine hours before police detained several opposition MPs and took them to New Police Lines at Kingsway Camp. Around 50 MPs were detained, while police figures put the total number of people detained at around 260.Rahul Gandhi questioned why elected representatives were being prevented from meeting the Election Commission when its office was only metres away. “If the representatives of the people cannot meet the Election Commission, then what is the meaning of democracy?” he said.After his release, Congress MP Pawan Khera warned that Tuesday’s protest was not the end of the opposition campaign against the CEC.“If Gyanesh Kumar thinks that just because we went home today, it is all over, he needs to understand that this is merely the beginning — nothing has ended yet,” Khera said.The lunch hosted by Kharge is therefore expected to serve as a meeting point for the alliance to discuss its immediate strategy and decide how to sustain pressure over the “vote chori” issue.The opposition has been demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation and is seeking a meeting with the election commissioners to press its allegations. articles.title: 'Like your movie, money is Ata Pata Laapata': SC directs Rajpal to pay Rs 2 crore by Oct 13
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday directed actor Rajpal Yadav to deposit Rs 2 crore towards the amount due to the complainant in a cheque-bounce
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Wednesday directed actor Rajpal Yadav to deposit Rs 2 crore towards the amount due to the complainant in a cheque-bounce case by October 13, saying it would consider his plea against the High Court order after the payment is made.Yadav, who was present in court, brought a demand draft of Rs 1.15 crore, while the remaining Rs 85 lakh is to be paid by October 13 through a buyer of his property, who was also present in court.The court, however, came down heavily on Yadav's conduct and warned that it could enhance his sentence, saying repeated extensions were being granted only to ensure that the complainant received the money.The Court said the deposit was directed to secure the amount due to the complainant and observed that Yadav’s conduct had not satisfied it.“Law should not be utilised like this”, the Court said.After passing the order, the bench had an informal exchange with Yadav, who spoke about the financial difficulties caused by his film Ata Pata Laapata. He said the film had resulted in losses of around Rs 200-250 crore and that the producers had also suffered losses.During the hearing, the Court also remarked in jest that the film's title was synonymous with Yadav's conduct.“Like your movie, your money is also Ata Pata Laapata, gayab”, the CJI said.Before the order was passed, film actor Rajpal Yadav appeared before the Supreme Court for the hearing of a cheque-bounce case against him and said, "The matter is before the honourable Supreme Court, and our legal team and lawyers will speak on the issue. I have the utmost respect for my country and for the Supreme Court. Whatever decision is taken by the court, wherever and whenever it is delivered, will be universally accepted."Yadav later greeted the bench, saying, “Pranam karta hoon,” and spoke about the losses of Rs 200-250 crore he had incurred over the film.The CJI advised him to make a good film and entertain people, adding in jest that advocates appearing before the Supreme Court were also good actors and could be cast in his films.Yadav's counsel told the Court that he had approached the Registry to make the payment, but RTGS was not permissible. He said the actor had therefore brought a demand draft of Rs 1.15 crore.On the remaining Rs 85 lakh, the counsel said a buyer of Yadav's property was present in court and the amount would be paid once the transaction was completed.Yadav submitted that the dispute arose from a Rs 5 crore liability connected with the film Ata Pata Laapata, while the film had caused much larger losses.The case arises from an alleged loan extended to Yadav by Murli Projects Pvt Ltd in 2010 for Ata Pata Laapata. Seven repayment cheques of Rs 1.05 crore each were subsequently dishonoured.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Billionaire Ron Burkle bought Frank Lloyd Wright’s earthquake-damaged Ennis House for about $4.5 million, roughly 70% below its original ask, then spent up to $17 million restoring it before it sold for $18 million
articles.summary: Billionaire investor Ron Burkle purchased Frank Lloyd Wright’s Ennis House in Los Feliz for about $4.5 million in 2011, roughly 70 percent below its
articles.body: Billionaire investor Ron Burkle purchased Frank Lloyd Wright’s Ennis House in Los Feliz for about $4.5 million in 2011, roughly 70 percent below its original asking price, after the landmark had been damaged by earthquakes and heavy rains. He then spent up to $17 million on a meticulous restoration that repaired structural cracks, rebuilt decorative concrete blocks and updated mechanical systems. In 2024, the fully restored home sold for $18 million, making it one of the most expensive Wright-designed residences ever sold, according to the Los Angeles Times and Architectural Digest. Read more details about it here:A textile-block masterpiece in Los FelizThe Ennis House sits on a ridge in Los Feliz, overlooking the city from a dramatic hillside site. Designed by Frank Lloyd Wright in 1923 and completed in 1924, it is the largest of his four textile-block houses in the Los Angeles area. The home is built from more than 27,000 interlocking concrete blocks, each cast with a geometric pattern that creates the distinctive Mayan-revival aesthetic for which the house is known.Wright conceived the textile-block system as a way to create beautiful, affordable homes using locally made concrete blocks reinforced with steel. The blocks are both structure and ornament in the Ennis House, with patterned faces on the exterior and interior walls. The result is a residence that’s both monumental and intricately detailed, a hallmark of Wright’s later California work. Over the decades, the Ennis House became an icon of Los Angeles architecture and a frequent filming location for movies and television. Its striking appearance and hillside location made it a natural choice for productions seeking a dramatic, otherworldly backdrop. That fame, however, also brought wear and tear, as the house hosted events and shoots that sometimes strained its aging structure.Earthquakes, rain and years of declineThe Ennis House suffered significant damage in the 1994 Northridge earthquake, which opened cracks in walls and destabilised portions of the structure. Further problems emerged in the winter of 2004 to 2005, when heavy rains saturated the hillside and triggered mudslides that threatened the foundation. Water infiltration and ground movement compounded the earthquake damage, leaving the house in a precarious condition. Clearly, by the time it was listed, the house would require a lot of restoration. The architectural importance of the house, as well as its choice location, justified the initial asking price of $15 million. However, the extent of the damage and the cost of repairs deterred many potential buyers, and the price was eventually reduced. Burkle’s purchase at about $4.5 million represented a steep discount, but it came with the understanding that millions more would need to be invested to save the house, as per the reports.The situation underscored a broader challenge facing many historic homes. Architectural importance does not equal financial viability, especially in the face of serious structural problems. Without a buyer willing to undertake a major restoration, the Ennis House would be at risk of further deterioration, or even partial loss. Burkle’s purchase ensured preservation, rather than abandonment or subdivision.A multi-year restoration effortBurkle assembled a team of architects, engineers and craftsmen to lead the restoration, with a focus on repairing the textile blocks and stabilising the structure. Cracks in walls were carefully injected with grout, and damaged blocks were removed, recast and reinstalled to match the original patterns. The goal was to preserve as much of Wright’s fabric as possible while ensuring the house could withstand future seismic events.Mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems were also upgraded to modern standards. The house was rewired and plumbed, the heating and cooling systems upgraded, and the drainage and waterproofing improved to keep water out. These were necessary upgrades to make the home livable by modern standards while maintaining its historic character. The restoration took more than a decade, with work continuing into the 2020s. Reports estimate that Burkle spent up to $17 million on the project, far more than his initial purchase price. That investment transformed the Ennis House from a damaged landmark into a fully restored residence that could once again serve as a private home and a showcase of Wright’s vision.From restoration to record sale The restored Ennis House went back on the market in 2024 with an asking price to match its restored state and importance as an architectural landmark. The property sold for $18 million, a figure that put it among the most expensive Wright-designed homes ever sold. The sale price was close to Burkle’s total investment when combining his purchase price and restoration costs, though it also represented a major milestone in the market for historic architecture.Architectural Digest noted that the Ennis House sale set a new benchmark for Wright properties, surpassing previous records for his residential work. The price reflected not only the design of the house but how much work it would take to return it to life. For buyers, the Ennis House is a rare chance to own a fully restored masterpiece by one of the greatest architects in American history. The sale also highlighted the role of private owners in preserving historic landmarks. Without Burkle’s willingness to invest serious money in restoration, the Ennis House might have continued to decay, or been altered in ways that could have compromised its integrity. His stewardship ensured that the house would be passed on in excellent condition, ready for the next chapter in its long history.A sign of preservation and possibilityThe saga of L.A.’s Ennis House shows how quickly architectural icons can fall apart when earthquakes, water damage and neglect set in. But its turnaround makes a bigger point: damaged history isn’t a lost cause if someone brings enough cash and patience to the table.In Los Angeles, the property is a point of great pride, a connection to visionary designers that defined the city’s identity. When Ron Burkle stepped in, he wasn’t just sealing a real estate deal, he was saving heritage that almost disappeared. His subsequent $18 million sale didn't magically erase years of costly repairs, but it proved iconic architecture holds value when cared for right. Now restored, the Ennis House enters a fresh new era.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Meet Kimberley Christopher, the Florida State doctoral candidate who developed a plasma process designed to destroy PFAS; after winning a collegiate pitch competition, she's now testing the tech through NSF I-Corps
articles.summary: A Florida State University doctoral candidate is trying to tackle one of the most persistent classes of environmental contaminants with a technology
articles.body: A Florida State University doctoral candidate is trying to tackle one of the most persistent classes of environmental contaminants with a technology designed not just to capture PFAS, but potentially destroy them. Kimberley Christopher, a doctoral candidate in Florida State University’s Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, has developed a patent-pending plasma process that uses electrons to trigger the breakdown of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, better known as PFAS or “forever chemicals.” After winning a collegiate startup pitch competition, Christopher is now testing the technology’s commercial potential through the National Science Foundation’s I-Corps program.The NSF-backed project, led by FSU chemical engineering professor Bruce R. Locke, is examining whether the technology can become a cost-competitive, energy-efficient way of destroying PFAS in water. The active I-Corps award runs from September 2026 through August 2027 and provides $50,000 in funding for the team to assess its translation and commercial potential.Why PFAS are difficult to destroyPFAS refers to a large class of human-made chemicals that have been used for decades because of their resistance to heat, water, oil and grease. They have been used in products ranging from nonstick cookware and stain-resistant materials to firefighting foams and some industrial applications. Their chemical stability, however, also makes many PFAS extremely difficult to break down once they enter the environment.US health authorities say 97% of people in US have measurable PFAS in their blood, while exposure can occur through contaminated drinking water, food, consumer products and contaminated sites. The US Environmental Protection Agency has also established drinking-water limits for several PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, reflecting concerns over their potential health effects.The challenge is not simply removing the chemicals from water. Some existing treatment approaches concentrate PFAS and transfer them into another material, leaving the contaminated substance to be managed or disposed of later. That is where Christopher's research takes a different approach.From capturing PFAS to breaking them downChristopher is working with Locke, FSU engineering innovation director Robert Wandell and chemistry professor Igor Alabugin on an electron-based framework for PFAS destruction.The approach uses nonthermal plasma and electrons to initiate chemical reactions that weaken the carbon-fluorine bonds characteristic of PFAS. According to the NSF project description, an electron injected into a PFAS molecule can trigger carbon-fluorine bond fragmentation, with the electron subsequently regenerated. The proposed mechanism therefore allows the electron to act catalytically rather than simply being consumed in the reaction.Research presented by Christopher and her FSU collaborators has focused on electron upconversion, a process intended to generate stronger reducing agents from relatively mild electron donors. Their computational work suggests that the approach can weaken carbon-fluorine bonds and promote degradation of certain PFAS compounds in nonthermal plasma systems.FSU called the resulting technology the Radi-Reactor plasma process. The university said it is designed to permanently destroy PFAS rather than merely transfer the contaminants from water into another waste stream. The distinction is important because Christopher's work is still in the research and commercialisation-validation stage. The technology is being evaluated through I-Corps to determine where it could work best and which customers would actually need it.30 interviews helped shape the ideaChristopher did not initially enter her doctoral program intending to become an entrepreneur. Her research is in computational physical organic chemistry, but a regional I-Corps program introduced her to the commercial side of scientific research.As part of the regional program, Christopher conducted 30 discovery interviews with potential users and stakeholders. The goal was to understand how organisations currently deal with PFAS contamination, what problems remain unresolved and which potential customer groups could benefit most from a destruction technology.PFAS contamination affects a wide range of industries and waste streams, making the customer-discovery process particularly important. The NSF project identifies possible applications including PFAS-rich landfill leachate, firefighting-foam waste, industrial wastewater and drinking water. Christopher's experience eventually took the technology from laboratory discussions to a competitive pitch.From pitch competition to NSF I-CorpsAfter completing the regional I-Corps program, Christopher was nominated by FSU's Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship to participate in the Florida Venture Forum Collegiate Pitch Competition. There, she presented the PFAS technology to investors, venture capitalists and other potential supporters. With support from FSU's IGNITE program, Christopher won first place, according to the university.The win helped move the project into the next phase. Christopher's team began the NSF's national I-Corps program in early September 2026. Unlike a conventional scientific research grant, I-Corps focuses heavily on customer discovery and determining whether a laboratory invention can become a viable product or business.The NSF describes I-Corps as a seven-week entrepreneurial training program designed to help scientists and engineers move promising inventions beyond the laboratory and toward commercialisation. Since its launch in 2012, more than 2,500 teams have participated, with nearly 1,400 subsequently launching startups, according to the NSF.100 interviews in seven weeksThe next stage is considerably larger than Christopher's first round of customer research. Her team plans to complete 100 discovery interviews over seven weeks, from September through October, as it investigates potential markets and identifies the customer segment most likely to benefit from the technology.The goal is not simply to prove that the chemistry works. Christopher also wants to determine where the process could have the greatest real-world impact and whether it can eventually compete on cost and efficiency with existing approaches. That distinction is central to the I-Corps process. The NSF says the program is designed to reduce the risks involved in moving technologies from laboratories into the marketplace by forcing researchers to test assumptions with potential customers and industry participants.Christopher hopes the work will eventually form the basis of a new company called Radical Solutions Corp. Her longer-term goal is to make the PFAS-destruction technology more effective and cost-competitive while finding applications where permanent destruction offers a clear advantage over simply concentrating or transferring the contaminants.For now, the FSU researcher is still at the crucial testing stage. The technology has not yet become a commercial PFAS treatment system, and its performance, economics and scalability remain subjects of ongoing evaluation.But the path from a doctoral research project to a statewide pitch competition and now a federally funded I-Corps program illustrates how university research can move toward the marketplace.For Christopher, the next test is no longer confined to the laboratory. It is whether a technology designed to break apart some of the most persistent chemicals in the environment can also solve a practical problem for the industries and communities dealing with them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Wyoming Army veteran fought a mountain lion bare-handed for 20 seconds to save his dog; said cat ‘put me right down’
articles.summary: An Army veteran from Cody, Wyoming, found himself in a fight with a juvenile mountain lion after the predator attacked his two-year-old Labrador
articles.body: An Army veteran from Cody, Wyoming, found himself in a fight with a juvenile mountain lion after the predator attacked his two-year-old Labrador retriever, Diesel, near the South Fork Road area outside Cody. Adam Borkhus had driven into the area hoping to photograph elk and was carrying bear spray and a pistol when he heard his dog yelp. He ran towards the sound and found the mountain lion on top of Diesel. Because the animals were entangled, Borkhus feared shooting could hit his dog, so he kicked the mountain lion. The animal immediately turned on him, knocked him to the ground and fought with him for roughly 20 seconds before fleeing. Borkhus suffered scratches, while Diesel escaped without significant injuries.How a Wyoming Army veteran's trip to photograph elk turned into a fightBorkhus had travelled with Diesel to the South Fork area near Cody, where he hoped to photograph elk. KTVQ reported that rainy weather had made him think the conditions could produce interesting photographs. He stopped near the Deer Creek Trailhead and let Diesel out of the vehicle. The situation changed within moments. Borkhus heard Diesel yelp and went to investigate, discovering a young mountain lion on top of his dog. The encounter occurred in heavy cover along South Fork Road, according to Wyoming Game and Fish officials.Borkhus already had two forms of protection with him. He was carrying bear spray and a pistol because of the presence of grizzlies in the area. However, the close-range struggle between Diesel and the mountain lion created another problem: either weapon could potentially injure his own dog.“There wasn’t time to think,” Borkhus told Cowboy State Daily, explaining that his immediate concern was protecting Diesel.The kick that made the mountain lion turn on himWith Diesel underneath the mountain lion, Borkhus decided to intervene physically. He kicked the animal, which caused it to turn away from the Labrador and towards him.The mountain lion then pounced on Borkhus and struck him in the chest, knocking him onto his back. The Wyoming man said he tried to keep the animal's mouth away from his neck and face while using his other hand to fight it. Borkhus estimated that the physical struggle lasted around 20 seconds, although KTVQ reported that he described the entire encounter as lasting less than 30 seconds. During the fight, he attempted to punch the mountain lion as it repeatedly swiped at him.Despite being much larger than the animal, Borkhus said he was surprised by its strength. He described himself as 6 feet 3 inches tall and 320 pounds and estimated that the juvenile mountain lion weighed no more than about 70 pounds.“He hit me in the chest and put me right down. That thing was strong,” Borkhus told Cowboy State Daily. The mountain lion eventually broke away and disappeared into the surrounding vegetation.Diesel escaped without serious injuryOnce the mountain lion fled, Borkhus discovered that Diesel had escaped the confrontation without significant injuries. The Labrador apparently had little interest in continuing the adventure. According to Borkhus, Diesel ran directly back to the vehicle and waited there while his owner recovered from the encounter. Borkhus later joked about his dog's reaction, saying Diesel appeared to be communicating that they should leave. He also said the experience did not seem to change the dog's personality. “Nope. He’s just his own dumb self,” Borkhus told Cowboy State Daily when asked whether Diesel had become nervous or behaved differently afterwards.Borkhus, meanwhile, was left with scratches on his face, hands and arms. KTVQ reported that the injuries were not severe enough to require stitches. The encounter nevertheless resulted in medical treatment. Borkhus received a tetanus booster and antibiotics, and doctors also began a precautionary course of rabies vaccinations.Wyoming Game and Fish investigated the encounterBorkhus contacted the Wyoming Game and Fish Department after the incident. Wildlife personnel responded that evening and searched the area for the mountain lion, but they were unable to locate it.Officials confirmed that a dog had been attacked in heavy cover along South Fork Road near the Deer Creek Trailhead, followed by an attack on a person. Based on their investigation, the department said the incident was most likely a surprise encounter that triggered aggressive defensive behaviour from the mountain lion. The department said it would continue monitoring the area.That assessment is significant because it distinguishes the incident from a mountain lion deliberately pursuing a person. Wyoming Game and Fish describes mountain lions as the state's most elusive large carnivore and says they are rarely seen.The department explains that their cryptic behaviour is linked to their successful stalking and ambush hunting strategy. Deer and elk are their primary food sources in Wyoming, although research has documented mountain lions eating other mammals, including porcupines, raccoons, beavers and coyotes.The animal involved in Borkhus's encounter was described as a juvenile. A representative of the Mountain Lion Foundation told Cowboy State Daily that a mountain lion of that size could potentially still be associated with its mother, since young lions generally remain with their mothers until around the age of two.What to do if a mountain lion appearsWyoming Game and Fish says conflicts between people and mountain lions are rare, but it provides specific advice for people travelling in lion habitat.The department recommends avoiding solitary recreation when possible because groups are more likely to make enough noise to prevent a surprise encounter. People should never approach a mountain lion and should give the animal a route to escape.If someone encounters a mountain lion, the department advises remaining calm and speaking in a calm, firm manner. The animal should not be chased or cornered.Most importantly, Wyoming Game and Fish says that if a mountain lion attacks, people should fight back and defend themselves. The department also asks people to report mountain lion sightings and encounters to wildlife authorities.The brief fight began with Borkhus trying to save his dog and ended with both the man and the Labrador making it back to their vehicle. Despite the frightening encounter, Borkhus indicated that he and Diesel planned to continue enjoying the outdoors together.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Your child does not have to become a champion: How sports can build resilience, discipline and confidence for life
articles.summary: As a sportsperson, coach, educator and now a parent, I have spent a large part of my life watching children play sports.
articles.body: As a sportsperson, coach, educator and now a parent, I have spent a large part of my life watching children play sports. And over the years, I am convinced of one thing: the child who walks onto a sports field is rarely the same child who walks off it a few years later.When parents choose a sport for their child, they often think about fitness, good health, medals or perhaps even future opportunities. But there is another question worth asking: What kind of experiences will this sport give my child, and what might they learn from them?Because sport can shape much more than physical ability. It can influence how children respond to pressure, failure, teamwork, criticism and success.More than a gameFrom a fairly early age, sports teach lessons that cannot always be taught in a classroom setting. A classroom can teach a child what resilience means. Sports make them experience it.Imagine a 12-year-old standing at the free throw line with her team one point behind. Or a young goalkeeper who has just conceded a goal because of his mistake. A swimmer who has trained for months but finishes fourth. A child sitting on the bench while a teammate starts ahead of them.What happens next?Do they try again? Do they blame somebody else? Can they congratulate the winner? Can they listen to their coach when they are disappointed? Can they return to training the next morning?These seemingly small sporting moments are actually enormous lessons in character.Research increasingly supports what those of us in sport have witnessed for years. A 2024 Women’s Sports Foundation study found that 67% of women who had participated in sports felt they carried the skills and lessons they learnt through sport into adulthood, including teamwork and leadership. Learning from mistakes and handling pressure were amongst the most important skills identified.A recent 2026 review focused on adolescent sports participation in India similarly highlights the role sport can play in developing teamwork, discipline, communication, resilience and decision-making. But statistics tell only part of the story. The real impact of sport is often seen in the small moments when children are tested, challenged or asked to try again.Different sports, different experiencesDifferent sports challenge children in different ways. In an individual sport, there is nowhere to hide. A tennis player cannot pass the responsibility to someone else after losing a point. A swimmer learns to compete against the clock and, often against themselves. Athletics teaches persistence and patience because improvement can come down to a fraction of a second.Team sports teach you that talent alone can never be enough. You have to communicate. You have to trust. Sometimes you lead, sometimes you follow. Sometimes the best things one does for their team never reflect on the scoreboard or the scoresheet.Sports constantly ask children to understand their role within something larger than themselves. And that is a powerful lesson in building one’s character and for life.Your child does not have to become a championIt's not always about winning.This is perhaps the part I wish more parents understood. Your child does not have to be exceptional at sport for sport to be exceptional for your child.Not every child who plays sport needs to play for India, or reach the nationals, or need a professional contract. Podium finishes or trophies are not the only return for the hours invested.Confidence is a return.Discipline is a return.Learning to accept criticism without falling apart is a return.Learning that somebody can be better than you today, and that you can still work to be better tomorrow is a return.Being passionate about your sport is a return.Learning how to keep your pride under victory is a return.But my personal favourite - learning how to lose - is one of the greatest lessons sports can teach a child. It is indeed one of the sport’s greatest life lessons. As parents, our instinct is naturally to protect our children from disappointment. Sports, time and again, give them small, manageable encounters with failure while they are young enough to learn how to deal with it.A missed shot is disappointing. Losing a final hurts. Not making a team can feel devastating. But life will eventually hand them bigger disappointments. Sports quietly prepare them for those days.Another important factor, especially for young children trying to play sport, is the adults they are surrounded by. Sports do not automatically build character. The environment around sport builds character. Multiple studies on youth sport have also cautioned that positive outcomes are not universal; coaches and parents have an important influence on whether the sporting environment develops confidence, connection and resilience or instead contributes to pressure or burnout.Children need competition. They need standards. They need to be held accountable. But they should also be given freedom to make mistakes.Our job as adults is not to remove every obstacle from their sporting journey. Sometimes our job is simply to allow them to encounter the obstacle and discover that they can overcome it themselves.Let them playAfter spending most of my life in sport, some of my strongest memories are not of medals or scoreboards.They are of early mornings, difficult practices, teammates who became family, coaches who demanded more from me, painful losses, and the feeling of getting up and trying once again.These experiences shape the athlete one becomes. More importantly, they shape the person one becomes.So when you choose a sport for your child, don’t only ask where it might take them. Ask what it might teach them along the way. Because long after the trophies gather dust and the final scores are forgotten, the resilience, discipline, courage, friendships and confidence developed through sport can remain.And perhaps that is sport’s greatest victory.(Raspreet Sidhu Former Captain, Indian Women's Basketball Team and Central Head - Sports: Shiv Nadar School)You use AI every day. articles.body: MUMBAI: The Maharashtra government on Tuesday dubbed as “fanciful’’ “irrelevant an superfluous” the contention by political parties Indian National Congress, Communist Party of India (CPI) and social activists of any likely misuse of its new Special Public Security Act and said neither petitioner showed how it has impingned their rights and hence they lack the requisite locus to challenge its constitutionality.“ Maharashtra, because of its highest urban population has ‘ become center of Maoist urban network’’ said the State and lacked a legal framework of public security Act to ban frontal organisations like other affected States, the government said in its reply to a batch of petitions.The perceived misuse of the Act is tackled within the Act itself said the State. The Advisory board will be headed by retired HC Judge and only after confirmation or by advisory board can an organisation be ‘banned’ and anycase it is subject to review before the HC as well.THE articles.title: Annamalai’s next political move? We The Leaders to launch Abdul Kalam centre to train 100 women
articles.summary: CHENNAI: Former IPS officer K Annamalai appears to be laying the groundwork for his next political move through We The Leaders, with the organisation set
articles.body: CHENNAI: Former IPS officer K Annamalai appears to be laying the groundwork for his next political move through We The Leaders, with the organisation set to launch the Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Centre for Ethics and Politics in Coimbatore and begin training around 100 women in grassroots leadership.The Centre, founded by Annamalai, will be inaugurated on October 15, with its first two-day Foundation Course starting the same day. The inaugural batch will comprise women from across Tamil Nadu, with priority given to those involved in We The Leaders’ grassroots, community and organisational activities.The initiative comes as Annamalai remains outside the BJP’s state leadership structure, with the new platform providing an organisational route to engage with grassroots workers and develop a pool of women trained in public leadership.The free training programme will cover grassroots leadership, ethics in public life, the Constitution, local governance, public policy, public finance, communication, strategy and organising. The focus will be on practical exercises, case studies, simulations and public problem-solving rather than classroom lectures alone.The Centre plans to subsequently offer a four-week Leadership Academy, followed by a 100-day Field Lab, enabling participants to apply their training to real community and public issues.The decision to begin with an all-women batch is being positioned as part of We The Leaders’ Month of Women Empowerment & Safety, with the organisation seeking to move women’s participation in public life beyond representation to leadership and decision-making.The Centre is expected to provide Annamalai with a new platform for political and grassroots engagement, even as its founders maintain that its broader objective is to develop ethical and responsible public leaders.The inaugural programme will be held at the Centre’s facility in Neelambur, Coimbatore.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: Video: Bengaluru footpath transformer explodes outside Amazon office, 2 injured
articles.summary: BENGALURU: A transformer box installed on a footpath outside Amazon’s office on Baglur Main Road exploded, injuring two pedestrians and raising questions

articles.body: MUMBAI: Mumbai Police have banned the bursting of firecrackers, fireworks and rockets on public streets and roads, besides prohibiting the use of laser lights and high-intensity light beams across the Brihanmumbai Police Commissionerate.The restrictions came into force from on October 6 and will remain effective until midnight on December 4, unless withdrawn earlier.The restrictionsThe police order follows directions issued by the Bombay high court on September 22 in suo motu PIL No. 1 of 2026.The court directed authorities to impose a total ban on bursting areas within the jurisdiction of the Brihanmumbai Police Commissionerate.Violators may face legal actionMumbai Police have warned that anyone contravening the order will be liable for penal action under applicable laws.Action may be taken under the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, Explosives Act, 1884, and articles.title: California couple says county entered their property for road-safety work, they spent $300,000 fixing alleged damage and then received a $676,703 bill; fresh federal court order keeps part of fight alive
articles.summary: A California couple who say Santa Clara County damaged their property while trying to deal with a landslide threatening a public road have been allowed to
articles.body: A California couple who say Santa Clara County damaged their property while trying to deal with a landslide threatening a public road have been allowed to continue parts of their legal fight. The couple say they spent more than $300,000 repairing the alleged damage, only to later receive a $676,703.22 bill from the county for its work. A federal judge has dismissed their current complaint but allowed them to amend some of their claims.Alejandro V Rubin and Lisa M Stein own property in an area designated as a “high-hazard landslide zone”, according to the court document. Their land includes a hillside overlooking Mount Madonna Road, a public road maintained by Santa Clara County. According to their complaint, a landslide began around March 2024, sending “soil and debris onto Mount Madonna Road”. The situation continued to worsen despite efforts by the couple and the county.In June 2024, the couple told the county that the landslide “posed an imminent threat to public safety”. The county then issued a Summary Abatement Order and entered the property to carry out remediation work. The couple alleged that the work caused substantial damage and “permanently destabilized the hillside”.Rubin and Stein said they spent more than $300,000 repairing hazardous conditions they alleged were caused by the county. They were later sent a $676,703.22 invoice for the county’s mitigation work. They filed their federal lawsuit in March 2026.Six claims against countyThe lawsuit named Santa Clara County, three county bodies and seven county officials. The couple brought six claims, including alleged violations of procedural due process, a Fifth Amendment taking, failure to train or supervise employees, inverse condemnation, dangerous condition of public property and negligence.The defendants asked the court to dismiss the case. During the proceedings, Rubin and Stein dropped their three state-law claims including inverse condemnation, dangerous condition of public property and negligence. They also sought permission to pursue claims against the named officials individually rather than in their official capacities.The court also removed the County Board of Supervisors, Planning and Building Department and Roads and Airports Department as separate defendants, finding that they were parts of Santa Clara County.Why notice claim was dismissedThe couple alleged that significant excavation work was carried out without “adequate notice or opportunity to appeal”. The county argued that the landslide presented an emergency and allowed officials to act without first holding a hearing.The judge pointed to the couple’s own statement that the landslide posed an imminent threat to public safety. Under California law, counties can take immediate action against a nuisance that poses a threat to public health or safety.The court therefore found that the county could begin the work without giving prior notice. It also said the couple still had an opportunity to seek an administrative hearing with the county.Other claims dismissedThe couple had also alleged that the county's actions amounted to a Fifth Amendment taking by depriving them of the use and enjoyment of their property. During the case, they sought to drop that argument and instead pursue a substantive due-process claim.The judge said the original claim had been presented as a takings claim and could not be changed into a substantive due-process claim at this stage. It was therefore dismissed.The court also dismissed their claim that the county failed to properly train or supervise employees. It found that the complaint did not provide enough facts showing that a county policy, practice or lack of training had caused a constitutional violation.Legal fight can continueUS District Judge Beth Labson Freeman's October 2 order dismissed the current claims but allowed the couple to amend several of them. The court said their lawyer had indicated that additional facts could be provided, meaning amendment would not necessarily be futile.Rubin and Stein can amend their procedural and substantive due-process claims, their failure-to-train or supervise claim and their claims against individual county officials. However, their Fifth Amendment takings allegations and three state-law claims cannot be amended.The couple must file an amended complaint within 45 days of receiving the Santa Clara County Board of Supervisors' final decision after an administrative hearing. The court also said failure to meet the deadline or correct the problems identified in the order would lead to the remaining claims being dismissed with prejudice.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1993, Bob Hope sold his 2,308-acre California ranch to the National Park Service for $16.7 million; the deal turned his former property into federal parkland and expanded protected land to about 20,400 acres
articles.summary: In 1993, comedian and entertainer Bob Hope sold his 2,308-acre Jordan Ranch in eastern Ventura County to the National Park Service for $16.7 million.
articles.body: In 1993, comedian and entertainer Bob Hope sold his 2,308-acre Jordan Ranch in eastern Ventura County to the National Park Service for $16.7 million. The acquisition added the rugged, oak-dotted property to the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area, bringing the park service’s holdings in the recreation area to about 20,400 acres, as per a report by Parade. Officials described Jordan Ranch as the crown jewel of the Simi Hills and the largest single acquisition within the recreation area at the time, according to various reports and project summaries. Read on to know more about it here:A ranch in the Simi HillsJordan Ranch sits in the Simi Hills east of Thousand Oaks, a landscape of rolling meadows, oak-lined canyons and grassy flats. The property includes Palo Comado Canyon and China Flat, areas that were praised for their natural beauty even before they became public parkland. Descriptions from the period refer to China Flat as a spectacular vantage point overlooking tiers of distant mountains, as per LA Times.Before the sale, the ranch had been eyed for development. Earlier proposals included luxury homes and a world-class golf course on parts of the property. The 1993 transaction ended those plans and ensured that the land would be preserved as open space. Park officials said the ranch would open for recreational use within four to six months, welcoming hikers, bikers and equestrians to terrain that had been privately held for decades.The sale also connected Jordan Ranch to adjacent protected land. The 2,308-acre tract abuts the 2,150-acre Cheeseboro Canyon property, which was already part of the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. As per LA Times, superintendents described the acquisition as preserving a key part of a wildlife corridor that runs from Simi Valley to the Pacific Ocean, allowing deer, bobcats and other large mammals to move between mountain ranges.Part of a larger conservation puzzleThe Jordan Ranch deal did not happen in isolation. It was tied to broader negotiations involving other Hope-owned properties and a major housing project known as Ahmanson Ranch. Under conditions set by the Ventura County Board of Supervisors, the Ahmanson development could not proceed until Hope’s other mountain tracts became public parkland. Those properties included the 4,369-acre Runkle Ranch near Simi Valley and the 339-acre Corral Canyon in Malibu.In 1990, Hope had signed an agreement to transfer about 5,700 acres of mountain property at three sites to a state parks agency for a below-market $20 million. That deal included Runkle Ranch, Corral Canyon and portions of Jordan Ranch, and it was described as one of the largest and most significant parkland transactions in recent Southern California history. The 1993 sale of Jordan Ranch to the National Park Service fulfilled part of that broader conservation framework. By 1991, a more complex arrangement had emerged. Hope agreed to a plan that would combine two giant housing projects near Simi Valley and turn more than 10,000 acres of mountain property into public parkland. Under that consolidated plan, park agencies would receive parklands worth between $120 million and $150 million, while Hope would sell 7,363 acres for a below-market $29.5 million. The Jordan Ranch sale in 1993 was a key step in making that vision a reality, as per reports.How the purchase came togetherThe final Jordan Ranch transaction followed more than five years of intense and ever-shifting negotiations. State park officials scrambled at times to secure federal funds before they expired, fearing the money might be redirected to other parkland acquisitions. At one point, the National Park Service signaled its intent to buy the 314-acre Paramount Ranch property in Agoura using money that had been set aside for Hope properties, adding urgency to the Jordan Ranch talks.Parade.com noted that Joseph T. Edmiston, executive director of the Santa Monica Mountains Conservancy, played a central role in engineering the $16.7 million purchase. He announced, as per the report, that the acquisition in June 1993 and said Hope would receive the Park Service’s payment within the next few days. Escrow was expected to close that Friday or the following Monday, marking the end of a long process that had involved developers, conservationists and local officials.The purchase price was widely reported as $16.7 million for the 2,308-acre ranch. That figure represented a significant investment in open space at a time when development pressure in the region was high. Edmiston described Jordan Ranch as a very critical parcel because it represented another key swath of protected wildlife habitat in the Santa Monica Mountains.From private ranch to public recreation areaOnce the sale closed, the National Park Service began planning how to manage the newly acquired land. Officials said getting the parkland ready for the public would cost about $120,000 in the first year, covering ranger patrols, road improvements, and the installation of gates and parking spaces. Blueprints for amenities such as restrooms, picnic tables and parking lots had not yet been drawn up at the time of the announcement.The entire property, including oak-lined Palo Comado Canyon and sage-carpeted China Flat, was expected to open for recreational use within months. Park officials anticipated that hikers, bikers and equestrians would quickly discover the rugged ranch, which had once been slated for luxury homes and a golf course. The opening marked a transition from private ownership to a space where the public could explore canyons, meadows and ridgelines that had been off limits for decades.The acquisition also had implications for nearby development. The Ahmanson Ranch project, a $1 billion plan to create a mini-city of 8,600 residents, remained contingent on Hope’s other properties becoming public parkland. The Jordan Ranch sale was a major accomplishment, but officials said the burden now fell on Ahmanson Land Co. to deliver two other Hope properties to park agencies if it wanted to build the housing project.A legacy of land and conservationBob Hope was one of the largest private landowners in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area during the early 1990s. His holdings included Jordan Ranch, Runkle Ranch and Corral Canyon, along with other parcels in the region. The series of deals he entered into with park agencies put thousands of acres into public ownership and helped shape the recreation area’s boundaries.In addition to the Jordan Ranch sale, Hope donated 360 acres of his Conejo Valley land to the Conejo Recreation and Park District. That property became the Hope Nature Preserve, a protected open-space area named in his honor. The combination of sales and donations ensured that a significant portion of his mountain land would remain undeveloped and accessible to the public.Today, Jordan Ranch is part of the Cheeseboro and Palo Comado Canyons Park section of the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area. The recreation area has grown to more than 150,000 acres and is often described as the world’s largest urban national park. The 1993 sale of Jordan Ranch remains a landmark moment in that growth, turning a celebrity-owned ranch into federal parkland and expanding protected land to about 20,400 acres at the time.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bass ‘horrified’ by Trump remarks about Los Angeles, San Diego
articles.summary: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) said she was “horrified” by President Trump’s remarks at a recent campaign rally that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego, saying a president should not speak of major U.S. cities as a potential cost of war. Trump defended the economic fallout from the Middle East conflict…
articles.body:
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) said she was “horrified” by President Trump’s remarks at a recent campaign rally that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego, saying a president should not speak of major U.S. cities as a potential cost of war.

Trump defended the economic fallout from the Middle East conflict to a crowd of GOP supporters in Nebraska earlier this week, appearing to suggest the Iranian regime could try to attack the U.S. with a potential nuclear weapon .

“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” Trump said at the Grand Island, Neb., rally. “They can take out a city — let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay.”

The rhetoric received swift backlash from several of California’s Democratic leaders , including Bass, who wrote on social platform X that his comment was “dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety.”

“The role of the president is to protect and defend the American people,” the mayor told CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Tuesday. “He went to war with Iran, and he basically said it’s OK, that it’s a small price to pay to attack 3.8 million people in the nation’s largest city.”

“I was horrified by those comments,” she added.

The comment was also criticized by California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), a possible contender for the 2028 presidential race, who called the president “deranged and dangerous” for what he described as Trump “saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego.”

The White House has since disputed the interpretation that Trump was promoting the idea that an attack on either city would be an acceptable price of the war.

White House communications director Steven Cheung said on social media Tuesday that Trump was instead arguing that confronting Iran had prevented the regime from posing a greater threat to the U.S. and blamed the media for misrepresenting the remark.

“The media freakout over President Trump’s comments is not rooted in reality,” Cheung said. “He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped.”

articles.title: California Democrats demand Trump apology for rally remarks
articles.summary: California Democratic lawmakers on Tuesday demanded President Trump apologize for remarks he made at a campaign rally suggesting Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego. “As members of the California Democratic Congressional Delegation, we call on President Trump to apologize to the over 16 million Americans who live in the Los Angeles and…
articles.body:
California Democratic lawmakers on Tuesday demanded President Trump apologize for remarks he made at a campaign rally suggesting Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego.

“As members of the California Democratic Congressional Delegation, we call on President Trump to apologize to the over 16 million Americans who live in the Los Angeles and San Diego metropolitan areas and all Americans who expect more out of our President,” the delegation, chaired by Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), said in a joint statement .

Lofgren was joined by the state’s 40 House members and Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) in responding to Trump’s comment earlier this week in Grand Island, Neb.

“Upon taking office, the president swears to uphold the Constitution and to protect us from our enemies,” the delegation wrote. “Yesterday, President Trump, while defending his unconstitutional war against Iran, appeared, incredibly to invite Iran to destroy two American cities.”

The Golden State lawmakers also reiterated what the president said verbatim: “Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego.” He added it was “a very small price to pay, and it’s [the conflict] going to be over with very soon,” defending the economic fallout from the Iran war.

Trump’s words also inflamed California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), who called the rhetoric “deranged and dangerous,” later adding that the comments were “dangerous –– if not treasonous” for suggesting the cities could be attacked.

The governor, who is weighing a 2028 presidential run , previously told The Hill that Trump is “mentally ill” and called for invoking the 25th Amendment. He also directed the State Threat Assessment Center to monitor for potential threats to both cities, noting that San Diego is home to one of the country’s largest U.S. Navy hubs.

The White House defended Trump’s remarks , with communications director Steven Cheung calling critics’ reaction a “media freakout.” The White House Rapid Response account on social platform X called the Los Angeles Times “buffoons” over its reporting on the comments, while White House spokesperson Davis Ingle called Newsom “the worst governor in America, and he may also be the dumbest.”

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass (D) told CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Tuesday that the remarks “horrified” her when Trump “basically said it’s OK, that it’s a small price to pay to attack 3.8 million people in the nation’s largest city.” San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria (D) urged the president to “keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”

“This is reckless, dangerous, and unhinged. Four million Angelenos are not bargaining chips,” Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman, who is seeking to replace Bass as mayor, wrote Tuesday in a post online .

California Republican House candidate Jim Desmond said he disagreed “vehemently” with the comments, emphasizing that Trump must “not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war.”

Desmond was the vice chair of the San Diego County Board of Supervisors and former mayor of San Marcos, part of San Diego County.
