articles.title: 3 years after Oct. 7, the world still thinks terrorism is someone else’s problem
articles.summary: On the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks, Sarri Singer argues that the global community must confront the universal threat of terrorism by calling it what it is, cutting off enemy funding, and treating survivor recovery as a matter of national security.
articles.body:
Wednesday marks three years since Oct. 7, the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust. When Hamas terrorists crossed into southern Israel, murdering roughly 1,200 people at a music festival , in their homes and in their beds, and dragging 251 hostages into Gaza, I knew what I was seeing.

I had seen it before. On June 11, 2003, a Hamas suicide bomber boarded my bus in Jerusalem and blew himself up, killing 17 people and wounding more than 100 . I survived. Two years earlier, on Sept. 11, I had been working just blocks from the World Trade Center.

These attacks shared a template for terror that the world has been slow to understand. Three years on, what have we learned? Sadly, not nearly enough.

Much of the world filed Oct. 7 under “the Middle East,” a story about one country and one conflict. That framing was comfortable, and wrong. The deliberate targeting of civilians, the livestreamed cruelty, the hostage-taking, the instant online celebration that turned atrocity into recruitment material: none of it was ever going to stay in one place. Terrorism studies what works and exports it.

Attacks inspired by the same ideology have struck far from Israel. On New Year’s Day 2025, an ISIS-inspired attacker drove a truck into crowds on Bourbon Street in New Orleans , killing 14. From Washington, D.C., to Manchester to Bondi Beach in Sydney, synagogues, Jewish events and ordinary public spaces became targets.

The script is by now familiar: shock, vigils, a brief debate about security failures. Then the world moves on, without confronting the jihadist network behind them and its ideology that justifies terrorism.

For more than two decades, I have sat with survivors of attacks in London, Paris, Mumbai, Bali, Boston and Israel. Their stories differ, but the lessons are strikingly similar. Three remain urgent.

First, call terrorism what it is, without qualifiers. After Oct. 7, some of the world’s most respected institutions struggled to use the word “terrorism” at all. Murdering families in their homes was described in terms of “resistance” or “context.”

Last week, when a pilot tried to crash a plane full of civilians , the media rushed to call it a “security incident” or a “scuffle in the cockpit” rather than the terrorist attempt it was. Blurring the line between grievance and murder tells future attackers their violence will be debated rather than condemned.

Second, stop funding your enemies. Terrorism is an enterprise, and enterprises run on money. The tunnels and rockets of Oct. 7 were built over years in a territory that received billions in international aid, while Hamas diverted concrete, fuel, and cash meant for civilians. The United Nations itself fired U.N. Relief and Works Agency staff over evidence that they had taken part in the massacre.

Too often, well-meaning donor money, through diverted aid or payments that reward attackers’ families, strengthens groups targeting the donors’ own citizens. I learned how hard this is to stop when I joined the parents of Taylor Force, an American killed in a terrorist attack in Israel , in suing my own government to enforce the law against one such program. Survivors should not have to go to court. Every democracy needs to double down on oversight that checks whom its foreign aid empowers.

Third, treat recovery as national security. Terrorists want more than to kill. They seek to instill fear, break families, and erode trust in the institutions meant to protect us. Nations have gotten better at the first hours after an attack. They remain terrible at what comes after. Survivors lose jobs, struggle with untreated trauma, and navigate a maze of agencies alone, long after the cameras leave. A society that visibly stands with its victims for the long haul is harder to terrorize.

Israel has, painfully, become the world’s most experienced practitioner in all three areas, and its advances in trauma and bereavement care since Oct. 7 offer lessons for everyone. Other nations needn’t agree with every Israeli policy to learn from that experience. Refusing to because of where it comes from is a luxury no government can afford.

Anniversaries invite speeches. I’d rather they invite accountability. On this third anniversary, the question isn’t only how we remember those murdered and kidnapped. It’s whether we will admit that what happened to them was not a regional tragedy, but a warning addressed to all of us, and whether we are finally ready to act like it.

Sarri Singer is founder and director of Strength to Strength, a nonprofit that unites international victims of terrorism and provides long-term psychological and peer support. She survived a terrorist bus bombing in Jerusalem in June 2003 and was a named plaintiff in Jackson et al. v. Trump et al., the lawsuit that led to a 10-year commitment by the State Department to enforce the Taylor Force Act .

articles.title: Vance: Iran must make ‘meaningful’ enrichment reduction to end war
articles.summary: Iran must do something “meaningful” related to its stockpile of enriched uranium to make progress in nuclear negotiations with the U.S., Vice President Vance said in an interview with Reuters on Tuesday. Iran’s claim of a right to enrichment is a key sticking point in negotiations over its nuclear program. While Iran says it does…
articles.body:
Iran must do something “meaningful” related to its stockpile of enriched uranium to make progress in nuclear negotiations with the U.S., Vice President Vance said in an interview with Reuters on Tuesday.

Iran’s claim of a right to enrichment is a key sticking point in negotiations over its nuclear program. While Iran says it does not seek to build a nuclear weapon, U.S. officials from both sides of the aisle say the Islamic Republic’s pursuit of stockpiles of highly enriched uranium is only for that purpose.

“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why ​do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched ⁠fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said in an exclusive interview with Reuters, while stumping for Republican candidates in Alaska.

“I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their ​enrichment capacity.”

The vice president is a key interlocutor in U.S. negotiations with Iran over its nuclear program, which are at an impasse over what the U.S. argues is confusion over who holds decisionmaking power in the Islamic Republic and tit-for-tat military strikes trying to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry pushed back on U.S. criticisms of a leadership crisis, and it blamed the Trump administration for failing to negotiate in good faith.

“The problem is actually the opposite: it lies in the contradictory positions and mixed messaging from US officials,” Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said at a weekly press conference, Reuters reported.

The U.S. launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28 with the stated goal of preventing Iran from building a nuclear weapon. But Iran has imposed huge costs on the U.S. and global economy by threatening shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, choking off a maritime route for about 20 percent of the world’s energy supplies.

Vance told Reuters that the U.S. is willing to strike an agreement where the Iranians commit to not rebuilding their nuclear program, which the Trump administration claims was destroyed in strikes carried out in June 2025.

“You ​know, what the president has said is, you know, look, from the very beginning, we’re willing ​to strike an agreement where the Iranians commit to not rebuilding their nuclear program ⁠and take real steps in order to do that, but it takes two to tango, and we’re not going to trade words for actions,” he said.

“In other words, the United States is not going to do things for mere promise of actions on the Iranian side. We need to trade actions for actions here, and we’ll see what the Iranians do.”

articles.title: US formally requests more information on death at Russia plague lab
articles.summary: The U.S. has sent a formal diplomatic complaint to the Russian government demanding more information regarding the death of a woman working at an antiplague research facility in Siberia and following reports of quarantine procedures, a source familiar told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. The Trump administration’s request came in the form of a demarche,…
articles.body:
The U.S. has sent a formal diplomatic complaint to the Russian government demanding more information regarding the death of a woman working at an antiplague research facility in Siberia and following reports of quarantine procedures, a source familiar told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network.

The Trump administration’s request came in the form of a demarche, an official diplomatic communication representing the U.S. position that can be used to protest or object to actions by a foreign government. The move signaled an escalation in efforts to receive credible information about the possible spread in Siberia of pneumonic plague, a highly infectious and fatal disease.

“We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government,” a State Department spokesperson told NewsNation when asked about the demarche.

“We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information.”

The demarche served to remind Russia of its obligations to share timely and complete public health information regarding dangerous infectious threats like plague to assess and prevent international spread, laid out in the World Health Organization’s (WHO) International Health Regulations.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Tuesday that it was “incumbent” on Russia to share more information with the world. He said initial information provided by Moscow did not warrant alarm, but “it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it, and we’re doing that.”

“We know what we know, obviously, about whatever the Russians have provided, which is it seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected, and there’s concern that that could have spread, at least internally. So you’ve seen them do quarantines with this — of that nature,” he said.

“But like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread. So we’re watching and monitoring it closely.”

The State Department on Tuesday refreshed its travel warning for Russia in response to concerns over plague spread, reminding Americans that there is a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” for Russia and that the U.S. has limited resources to assist Americans in the country.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Tuesday that his organization has been “actively following up” since a person died after being hospitalized with severe pneumonia in Irkutsk Oblast in Siberia.

“Initial media reports suggested pneumonic plague following an alleged accidental laboratory exposure,” Tedros said in a statement.

“In response to WHO’s verification request under the International Health Regulations, the Russian health authorities reported that no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk oblast,” he continued.

The WHO has also stated that the risk to the general population appears low.

Russian officials have sought to reassure the public over the past few days, The Moscow Times reported .

Initial reports described a female employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East hospitalized Sept. 29 with symptoms of severe pneumonia who died Thursday.

The lab worker was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology,” according to a statement from consumer safety watchdog Rospotrebnadzor cited by Interfax, the Times reported.

And nearly 200 people were placed under medical observation for suspected contact with the deceased, the Times reported .

Rospotrebnadzor said laboratory analysis of material from the patient did not reveal any microorganisms associated with her work handling dangerous pathogens, the Times reported.

articles.title: What 3 years of destruction in Gaza actually looks like
articles.summary: After watching the horrors Israel has inflicted on Gaza for three years, it’s time for the world to finally put a stop to it.
articles.body:
Today marks three years since the start of Israel’s devastating war on Gaza following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks , and one year since a ceasefire agreement that did nothing to halt Israel’s military . I want to tell you what three years looks like, because the number itself has stopped meaning anything to most people.

To understand what three years of this reality means, you have to look past the numbness of the passage of time and into the systematic dismantling of human life. When the United Nations reports that 90 percent of Gaza’s population has been forcibly displaced , it means nearly 2 million Palestinians have been uprooted, many of them violently displaced again and again. Most are now crammed into overcrowded, suffocating, unsanitary tent cities where the air smells of smoke and raw sewage, and where desperation is the only constant.

They aren’t just “displaced,” either — there is quite literally nothing left to go home to. With more than 80 percent of all buildings in Gaza systematically razed to the ground , entire family lineages, neighborhoods and childhood memories have been ground into gray concrete dust.

It looks like a child who has spent years flinching at incoming missiles and watching parents and siblings killed in front of them. The U.N. estimates that 17,000 children in Gaza have been orphaned or separated from their caregivers . Thousands more are living with amputations, burns and shrapnel wounds, and cannot get the surgeries or prosthetics they need. Even since the ceasefire, Israeli strikes and gunfire have continued to kill them, more than 300 children since it began.

It looks like a child who has never turned on a faucet and had water come out. Water, for that child, comes from a jerrycan, carried, rationed, fought for in a line. It looks like a child who doesn’t know that a roof is supposed to keep the rain out, not shake, leak and let the water in with the noise. It looks like a child who has never sat in an actual classroom, and who goes to bed hungry because there still isn’t enough food to fill him.

And it looks like an elderly man, like my father, diagnosed with cancer this fall and unable to get the treatment that could save his life, because Israel has destroyed the hospitals that could treat him and won’t let him leave Gaza for care that might.

This systematic tearing down of every wall, every hospital and every tree is not a byproduct of war. It is a deliberate effort by Israel to erase the very possibility of life for Palestinians in Gaza, leaving families with a cruel choice: abandon the soil of your ancestors, or die beneath its ruins.

In comfortable, air-conditioned halls of power, senior Israeli officials speak openly of “voluntary migration” of Palestinians from Gaza, saying that they’re waiting for President Trump to approve their plans. It is a sterile, dishonest term meant to mask a systematic uprooting — in other words, an ethnic cleansing — of an entire people from the only home they have ever known.

More than 71,000 children under five are currently at risk of acute malnutrition . Aid flows into Gaza have dropped by roughly one-third since the first months after the ceasefire, according to the U.N.

Meanwhile, the Israeli military is actively hauling away the rubble, trucking off concrete that has become one with the crushed bodies of Palestinians killed beneath it. International experts and U.N. officials say Israel isn’t just clearing away debris — they are clearing away a mass grave and evidence of Israel’s crimes.

We are told there is a ceasefire, but nothing has stopped in the underlying machinery of what human rights groups and other experts have concluded is a genocide carried out by Israel.

After watching the horrors Israel has inflicted on Gaza for three years, it is finally time for the world to put a stop to it. The U.S. and other signatories to the Genocide Convention are legally obligated to act. States must impose sanctions and an arms embargo on Israel, including ending unconditional U.S. military funding.

Israel must allow the unconditional entry of humanitarian aid — water, food, fuel, medicine and shelter materials. The United Nations Relief and Works Agency’s funding must be restored , and it must be allowed to work without interference; a patchwork of soup kitchens and charities cannot substitute for the civil infrastructure of an entire population.

And Palestinians must be centered in planning Gaza’s future — not a technocratic committee reporting to a board of foreign financiers who don’t have their best interests at heart.

My father did not survive a genocide only to die of untreated cancer in a shelter he has to flee every time it rains. To ask for more than that is not a radical demand — it is the floor of human decency. It is time our government started treating it like one.

Hani Almadhoun is vice president of philanthropy at UNRWA USA and co-founder of the Gaza Soup Kitchen. He is the author of the forthcoming book, “A Ladle against the Drones: One Family’s Fight to Feed Gaza.”
